This page states the methodology implemented by CompStats, as published in @Nava-Munoz2024. Each section gives a definition, its formula and the CompStats call that
computes it.

## Setting

A competition provides a gold standard $y$ of size $n$, kept by the organizers, and the predictions
$\hat{y}_1, \ldots, \hat{y}_m$ of $m$ systems. A performance measure $s(y, \hat{y})$ ranks the
systems. The quantity of interest is the performance $\theta_j$ of system $j$ on the population
from which the test set is assumed to be a random sample. The value computed on the test set is an
estimate of it. The setting imposes three constraints: there is a single dataset of fixed size,
the number of submissions is small, and only the predictions are available, not the algorithms.

## Bootstrap

Bootstrapping draws conclusions about the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the
data with replacement [@Chernick2011; @Efron1994]. In CompStats,
$B$ samples of $n$ indices are drawn with replacement from $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, and the measure is
computed on each sample for every system, which gives the bootstrap distribution
$s_j^{*1}, \ldots, s_j^{*B}$ of system $j$. The article uses $B = 10{,}000$, whereas the package default
is `num_samples=500`. This value is set with the parameter `num_samples` of every function of
`CompStats.metrics` and of `Perf`.

## Standard error and confidence interval

The standard error of the measure is the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution
(`Perf.se`). The $1-\alpha$ confidence interval is the percentile interval

$$
\left[ q_{\alpha/2}(s_j^{*}),\; q_{1-\alpha/2}(s_j^{*}) \right],
$$

where $q_p$ is the $p$-th quantile of the bootstrap distribution and $\alpha = 0.05$ by default
(`Perf.ci`).

## Comparison through independent samples

For two systems $i$ and $j$, with $i \neq j$, the comparison tests the null hypothesis
$H_0: \theta_i = \theta_j$ against the alternative $H_1: \theta_i \neq \theta_j$. If the
confidence intervals of the two systems do not overlap, there is a significant difference between
their performances. Conversely, if they partially overlap, there is some possibility that the performances of
the two systems are the same in the population. The latter case motivates the paired comparison
described next. `Perf.plot()` draws the intervals of the systems, ordered by performance.

## Comparison through paired samples

Every bootstrap sample contains the gold standard and the prediction of every system for the same
elements. Therefore, the difference in performance can be computed on each sample (the paired
bootstrap). For a system $A$ and a system $B$, the bootstrap distribution of the difference is

$$
\delta^{*} = s^{*}(y, \hat{y}_A) - s^{*}(y, \hat{y}_B).
$$

If the confidence interval of the difference contains zero, the hypothesis that both systems
perform equally cannot be rejected. `Perf.difference()` returns the differences between the best
system and each of the others, or with respect to the system named by the argument `wrt`, and
`Difference.plot()` draws their intervals.

## Statistical significance

Let $\delta(x) = \theta_A(x) - \theta_B(x)$ be the difference observed between systems $A$ and $B$
on the test set $x$. The null hypothesis $H_0$ states that $A$ is not better than $B$ in the
population. The p-value is

$$
p\left(\delta(X) > \delta(x) \mid H_0, x\right),
$$

where $X$ ranges over test sets of size $n$. Traditionally, if the p-value is below 0.05, the
observed difference $\delta(x)$ is considered sufficiently unlikely under $H_0$ to reject it, in
which case the evidence suggests that $A$ is superior to $B$. The exact p-value is in general hard
to compute and must be approximated. The paired bootstrap is widely used for this purpose
[@Koehn2004; @Berg-Kirkpatrick2012] and applies to any performance measure.
Following @Berg-Kirkpatrick2012, the p-value is estimated as the fraction of bootstrap samples in which the difference exceeds
$2\delta(x)$. The bootstrap distribution is centred on $\delta(x)$ rather than on zero because the
samples are drawn from $x$. `Difference.p_value()` returns these p-values.

## Multiple comparisons

Comparing the best system with each of the other $m-1$ systems tests the hypotheses
$H_0^j: \theta_1 \le \theta_j$ against $H_1^j: \theta_1 > \theta_j$, for $j = 2, \ldots, m$,
simultaneously, which inflates the probability of a Type I error. Correcting the p-values serves to
control the Type I error, to avoid spurious findings and to preserve the validity of the research.
Three corrections are
considered, all of which adjust the p-values. Bonferroni is conservative and multiplies each
p-value by the number of comparisons. Holm's step-down procedure adjusts the p-values
sequentially [@Holm1979]. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate [@Benjamini1995].
In CompStats they are selected with
`Difference.p_value(correction='bonferroni')`, `'holm'` and `'fdr_bh'`, respectively, or with any
other method accepted by `statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests`. The same `correction`
argument is accepted by `Perf.plot` and `Difference.plot`. When a `Perf` holds several measures,
each measure is corrected as its own family.

## Competitiveness of a competition

The competitiveness of a competition is evaluated with three aspects. The first is the number of
ties between systems in relation to the number of possible comparisons, which is $m(m-1)/2$ for
$m$ participants. A large proportion of ties indicates a higher level of competitiveness. The
second is the coefficient of variation of the participants' performance,
$CV = 100\, s_x / \bar{x}$, where $s_x$ is the sample standard deviation and $\bar{x}$ the mean.
A smaller $CV$ means greater competitiveness. The third is the distance between the winner and the
competitor in the middle of the table, $|win. - med.|$. A smaller distance indicates a smaller gap
between them.

The potential for improvement of a task, considering its measure, is assessed separately with the
possible percentage improvement,

$$
PPI = 100\,(1 - x_{winner}),
$$

where $x_{winner}$ is the score of the winner. The $PPI$ is higher when the gap between the
performance of the winner and the ideal value of the measure is large. It applies to scores where
the highest value is the best and the scores are capped. When a competition has a low $PPI$,
achieving substantial improvements is more challenging. It is a measure of the room for
improvement, not of competitiveness.

The summary tables of the article also report the number of ties with the winner without
correction and with the Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections, and the $CV$ is not
analysed for the mean absolute error, due to the nature of that measure. These indicators are
computed by the earlier DataFrame-based interface,
`CompStats.performance.performance_multiple_metrics`, documented in the [developer
docs](https://ingeotec.github.io/CompStats/dev/performance_api.html).

## Scope and assumptions

The inference assumes that the test set can be treated as a random sample of the population of
interest. Therefore, the intervals and the tests must be read in light of how the test set was built. The
methodology applies to any measure computed from a gold standard and predictions, for
classification and for regression. Measures where smaller is better, for example the mean absolute
error, are handled through the `BiB` (bigger is better) flag, which every function of
`CompStats.metrics` sets for its measure.
